exampleAnswers.title: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=xe^{3(x-1)}$ for $x\in[0,5),$ and let $f(x)$ be the odd extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-5,5).$ What is the value of $f(-1)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,5),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,5), \\[5pt] -F(-x), & x\in(-5,0). \end{cases} \]

In our cases, for $x\in(-5,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= -F(-x) \\[5pt] &= -(-x)e^{3(-x-1)} \\[5pt] &= xe^{3(-x-1)}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f(-1) &= (-1)e^{3(-(-1)-1)} = -e^{3(0)}= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{-1}. \end{align*}

example.title: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=x^2-2x$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the odd extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in(-\pi,0)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] -F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= -F(-x) \\[5pt] &= -((-x)^2-2(-x)) \\[5pt] &= -(x^2+2x) \\[5pt] &= -x^2-2x. \end{align*}

example.title: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=-x^2+5x$ for $x\in[0,8),$ and let $f(x)$ be the odd extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-8,8).$ What is the value of $f(-3)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,8),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,8), \\[5pt] -F(-x), & x\in(-8,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-8,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= -F(-x) \\[5pt] &= -(-(-x)^2+5(-x))\\[5pt] &= -(-x^2-5x) \\[5pt] &= x^2+5x. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f(-3) &= (-3)^2+5(-3)= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{-6}. \end{align*}

example.title: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=-2x^3+3x$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the odd extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in\left(-\pi, 0\right)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] -F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in\left(-\pi, 0\right),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= -F(-x) \\[5pt] &= -\big(-2(-x)^3+3(-x)\big) \\[5pt] &= -\big(2x^3-3x\big) \\[5pt] &= -2x^3+3x. \end{align*}

example.title: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=x^2-6x$ for $x\in[0,12),$ and let $f(x)$ be the odd extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-12,12).$ What is the value of $f(-4)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,12),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,12), \\[5pt] -F(-x), & x\in(-12,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-12,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= -F(-x) \\[5pt] &= -((-x)^2-6(-x))\\[5pt] &= -(x^2+6x) \\[5pt] &= -x^2-6x. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f(-4) &= -(-4)^2-6(-4)= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{8}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin(nx) \] Let $F(x)=2$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier sine series of the odd $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $b_n.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by \[ b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=2$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

\begin{align*} b_n &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi 2\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4}{n \pi} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_0^\pi \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{4}{n \pi} \left( \cos(n\pi) - \cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4(1-\cos(n\pi))}{n \pi}. \end{align*}

Finally, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ b_n = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{4(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n}}. \]

example.title: Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin(nx) \] Let $F(x)=-4$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier sine series of the odd $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $b_n.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by \[ b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=-4$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

\begin{align*} b_n &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (-4)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{8}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{n \pi} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_0^\pi \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8}{n \pi} \left( \cos(n\pi) - \cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8(\cos(n\pi)-1)}{n \pi}. \end{align*}

Finally, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ b_n = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{8((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n}}. \]

example.title: Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin(nx) \] Let $F(x)=6x$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier sine series of the odd $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $b_n.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by \[ b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=6x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ b_n = \dfrac{12}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=x \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 1 \\[3pt] v' = \sin(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = -\dfrac{1}{n}\cos(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} b_n &= \dfrac{12}{\pi} \left( uv \, \Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{12}{\pi} \left( -\dfrac{1}{n} \big[ x\cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} + \dfrac{1}{n} \int_0^\pi \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{12}{\pi} \left( -\dfrac{1}{n}\left(\pi\cos(n\pi)-0\cdot\cos(0)\right) + \dfrac{1}{n}\left[\dfrac{1}{n}\sin(nx)\right]_0^\pi \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{12}{\pi} \left( -\dfrac{\pi\cos(n\pi)}{n} + \dfrac{1}{n^2}\left(\sin(n\pi)-\sin(0)\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{12\cos(n\pi)}{n}. \end{align*}

Finally, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ b_n = -\dfrac{12(-1)^n}{n} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{12(-1)^{n+1}}{n}}. \]

example.title: Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.
question.explanation:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by \[ b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ b_n = -\dfrac{6}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=x \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 1 \\[3pt] v' = \sin(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = -\dfrac{1}{n}\cos(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} b_n &= -\dfrac{6}{\pi} \left( uv \, \Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{6}{\pi} \left( -\dfrac{1}{n} \big[ x\cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} + \dfrac{1}{n} \int_0^\pi \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{n\pi} \left( \left( \pi\cdot\cos(n\pi) - 0\cdot\cos(0) \right) - \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ \sin(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{n\pi} \left( \pi\cos(n\pi) - \dfrac{1}{n} \left( \sin(n\pi)-\sin(0) \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6\cos(n\pi)}{n}. \end{align*}

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ b_n = \dfrac{6(-1)^n}{n}. \]

Finally, the Fourier sine series is \[ f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{6(-1)^n}{n}} \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\sin(nx)}. \]
